title: Intelligent Agents & Environments
html:
An agent perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators. Describing an AI problem starts by pinning down four things — its PEAS — and the properties of its environment, which decide which techniques will work.

Environment
→
Sensors → percept
→
Agent program
→
Actuators → action
→
Environment

Agent function — a mapping from every possible percept sequence (everything the agent has perceived so far) to an action. The agent program is the concrete code that implements it on a machine.

Rational agent — for each possible percept sequence, selects the action expected to maximise its performance measure, given the evidence of the percepts and its built-in knowledge.

Watch out

Rational ≠ omniscient ≠ perfect. A rational agent maximises expected performance with the information it has; bad luck doesn't make it irrational. It should also gather information (look before crossing) and learn to compensate for incomplete prior knowledge.

The vacuum world

The textbook toy: two squares, A and B, each clean or dirty. The agent perceives (location, status) and can Suck, move Left or Right. The performance measure awards one point per clean square per time step:

Properties of task environments

DimensionEasy endHard endWhat it changes
ObservabilityFully observable — sensors show the whole relevant statePartially observable — noisy sensors, hidden stateHidden state → agent must keep internal state / beliefs
AgentsSingle-agentMulti-agent — competitive or cooperativeOpponents → game theory, adversarial search
DeterminismDeterministic — next state fixed by state + actionStochastic (nondeterministic) — outcomes uncertainUncertainty → probabilities, expected utility
EpisodesEpisodic — each decision independent (classify one image)Sequential — actions affect the future (chess)Sequential → planning ahead
ChangeStatic — world waits while agent thinksDynamic — world changes meanwhileDynamic → time pressure, anytime algorithms
State/timeDiscrete — finite states and actionsContinuous — positions, speedsContinuous → optimisation, control theory
KnowledgeKnown — rules/physics givenUnknown — must learn how the world worksUnknown → exploration, learning
TaskObservableAgentsDeterministicEpisodicStaticDiscrete
Crossword puzzleFullySingleYesSequentialStaticDiscrete
Chess with a clockFullyMultiYesSequentialSemiDiscrete
PokerPartiallyMultiStochasticSequentialStaticDiscrete
Taxi drivingPartiallyMultiStochasticSequentialDynamicContinuous
Image classificationFullySingleYesEpisodicStaticContinuous
Key point

The real world is the hard end of every dimension: partially observable, multi-agent, stochastic, sequential, dynamic, continuous and unknown. Most techniques in these notes relax one or more dimensions — search assumes fully observable + deterministic + known; MDPs drop determinism; reinforcement learning drops “known”.

What does PEAS stand for?

Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors — the four things to specify before designing an agent.

Is a rational agent always successful?

No. It maximises expected performance given its percepts and knowledge. With partial information or a stochastic world it can make the best possible choice and still get a bad outcome.

What's the difference between the agent function and the agent program?

The agent function is the abstract mathematical mapping from percept histories to actions (often an infinite table). The agent program is the finite code running on the agent's architecture that implements it.
